utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. Good afternoon, everyone in and around the courtroom. This is case number IT-08-91-T, the Prosecutor versus Mico Stanisic and Stojan Zupljanin.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. Good morning to everyone. May we begin by taking the appearances for the day, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. For the Prosecution, I'm Tom Hannis; along with one of our interns, Nedim Muminovic; and our case manager, Sebastiaan van Hooydonk.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Slobodan Zecevic, Slobodan Cvijetic, Eugene O'Sullivan, and Ms. Isabel Düsterhöft appearing for Stanisic Defence this morning. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours, Dragan Krgovic, Aleksandar Aleksic, and Miroslav Cuskic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. President, Your Honours, my learned colleagues on both sides, everyone in the courtroom. My name is Aleksandar Lazarevic and I will represent Mr. Tomislav Kovac, who is about to start his evidence today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you. If there are no housekeeping matters, would the usher please escort today's witness to the stand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Good morning, sir. Would you please make the solemn declaration that's on the card the usher's now handing to you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you. You may be seated. And although it may be apparent from your responses to me thus far, would you please confirm for the record that you're hearing me in a language that you understand.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I confirm that I can hear you in the language that I understand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Well, I would, first of all, thank you for accepting our invitation to assist us by appearing before the Tribunal. As would have been pointed out in the letter that you would have received from me writing on behalf of the Tribunal, you've been called as a witness by the Chamber itself, not by either side in this matter. And the questions that the Chamber has of you will be led by Judge Delvoie, who is at my right, and I would now pass the matter over to him. Judge Delvoie.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please, for the Judge.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Does this work? It seems to. Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Kovac.

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV KOVAC
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Can I begin to ask you to state for the record your full name and date and place of birth, please.

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV KOVAC
utterances.text: My name is Tomislav Kovac. I was born on the 4th of December, 1959, in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Before we proceed any further, I am informed that you have present here with you Mr. Lazarevic as counsellor for the purposes of your testimony in this case and that's pursuant to our order of 16 February 2012. Can you confirm that?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV KOVAC
utterances.text: Yes, I can.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Kovac, what is your ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV KOVAC
utterances.text: I am a Serb.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Is this the first time you testify before this Tribunal or have you ever testified before?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV KOVAC
utterances.text: This is my first testimony before this Tribunal. I hadn't testified before.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Did you testify before any of the courts in the region about the matters relating to the war?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV KOVAC
utterances.text: Yes, I gave evidence before the Court of Bosnia and Herzegovina on two occasions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Let me explain very briefly to you the proceedings before this Court. You have been called as a Chamber witness, and the Chamber thinks that it will -- it can finish your examination-in-chief within two hours. After that, there will be cross-examination by OTP, by the Defence of Mr. Stanisic and by the Defence of Mr. Zupljanin. And we hope to be able to finish your testimony by tomorrow, end of the hearing. We sit in the morning from 9.00 to a quarter to 2.00, and we have breaks every one hour and a half. That's for technical reasons, the tapes have to be changed and so on. But if there is for any personal convenience you need another break or you need whatever, please let us know and we will accommodate you. I would also like to inform you that the questions the Chamber has of you today pertain to the two accused in this case, Mr. Stanisic and Mr. Zupljanin. It is not the intent of this Chamber to compel you to answer questions that may affect your rights. The appointment of Mr. Lazarevic was made for exactly that purpose. However, the Chamber does expect you to be candid and forthcoming with your answers here today. Is that understood? Did you understand what I tried to explain to you?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV KOVAC
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: I would also like to mention to you that we are at the final phase of this case, and we heard already quite some evidence, practically all evidence that will be in this case. So the Trial Chamber has good knowledge of the context, and that is to allow you to focus very much on the precise questions we ask you without wandering off in contextual explanations. Okay? With that settled, could you please briefly tell us about your relevant educational background, very brief, please.

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV KOVAC
utterances.text: I finished elementary and secondary schools in Sarajevo, the secondary school of engineering. I graduated from the Belgrade university in criminology. At the time it was called the Higher School for the Interior. At the faculty of security in Skopje, I acquired another degree. And also in Skopje, I was nearing my post-graduate studies; however, I did not manage to do my magisterial thesis because the war broke out. I finished the School of State Security in Belgrade and at the time I was also involved in sports. I finished all the available training courses in martial arts and special units training that were available at the time while the former Yugoslavia was still functioning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you. And your professional background until 1991, please? Very briefly, again.

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV KOVAC
utterances.text: Following the completion of the studies of criminology, I had a scholarship, and therefore I started working for the State Security Service at the covert operations department. After a series of successful tasks in 1984, I was appointed chief inspector for state security of Bosnia-Herzegovina. In 1986, I was transferred to the public security service as the chief of police in Novi Grad in Sarajevo. Up until the first multi-party elections is the period when I was dismissed from that position and I was put on stand-by. After that, I became the chief of the police station at Ilidza and that is where I was when the war started. Well, that would be as far as my career prior to the war is concerned. As I said, in 1992 I became the chief of police station in Ilidza until August; and then in August I was appointed assistant minister of the interior in charge of police. In September of 1993 until 31st December 1994, I was an acting minister. And then in 1994 I became the chief of the public security service. In January 1995 - I can't give you the exact date - I became deputy minister of the interior, and in that same year, September 1995, I was appointed minister of the interior, which is the office that I held until December of that same year, which is when I was dismissed and when my service in the MUP of Republika Srpska was terminated, although pro forma I remained there in the capacity of an advisor.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. Can the Registrar please pull up P599. Witness, Mr. Kovac, in your binder, that is tab 4. Can you please look at this document and confirm, if you can, that this is your letter of appointment as an assistant minister.

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV KOVAC
utterances.text: Yes, I can confirm that this is the decision based on which I was appointed assistant minister.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kovac, is it correct that in October 1992 also you were designated the acting minister of interior by Mr. Stanisic in order to act on his behalf in his absence?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV KOVAC
utterances.text: As far as I remember, I was authorised by Mr. Stanisic. Since the post of deputy minister did not exist, he said that I could stand-in for him; and for that purpose he gave me certain authorities. Given the specific role of the minister during the war, I was entitled that in certain areas and certain lines of duty, I would act on his behalf inasmuch as he was able to delegate his authorities upon me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you look at tab 5 in your binder and tell us whether this document is to confirm that assignment.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, if I may be of assistance, there is a binder if you would like to use it. I have two --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: You have two?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Okay. So the witness has the binder now? It's tab 5. And the document number so that we can put it up on the screen is 0670-5858.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can confirm that I have seen this and that it is correct that Stanisic authorised me --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV KOVAC
utterances.text: -- to act on his behalf and to discharge the duties of minister. But I would like to add that I was not de facto deputy minister. The only body that could appoint deputy minister was the government. But, in fact, we had this kind of mutual relationship, in that he delegated some of his powers upon me so that I can perform the duties of the minister of the interior.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Kovac. That's why I used the term "designation" and not the term "appointment." Can you tell us for how long this order was in force, for how long did you act on behalf of this designation?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV KOVAC
utterances.text: Only for as long as Mr. Stanisic was the minister. After he was replaced by Ratko Adzic, I didn't have any decision, either factual or formal, one similar to this one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: And that was when exactly?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV KOVAC
utterances.text: That was towards the end, or rather, on the 1st of January, 1993, when the ministers were replaced. So, in other words, that would mean up until the end of 1992 I had this authority, that is, while the government in which Mr. Stanisic was the minister was in office.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you. And did you ever use this authority? Did you ever act as minister on behalf of Mr. Stanisic?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV KOVAC
utterances.text: Well, certainly that was in operational sense and by the nature of things that were inevitably happening, there were times when I had to submit reports to the Government of Republika Srpska or intervened in some personnel affairs or get involved in some operational tasks. So I used these powers at certain times, and it was only normal. In such institutions there's always someone who can always stand-in for someone who is number one, although that person is not appointed by the government. I think that Mr. Stanisic needed to have such an individual because the ministry was scattered around during the war. That's what the circumstances were at the time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. And a last question or it's, rather, a request about this document. Could you read it aloud, please, so that it can be translated for the record. Just read it aloud.

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV KOVAC
utterances.text: "Republika Srpska, Ministry of the Interior, Bijeljina. "Number 10-2-75/92. "Date: 21st October 1992. "Authorisation. "Whereby Mico Stanisic, the minister of the interior, authorises the assistant minister for the jobs and duties of the police Tomo Kovac to perform all the ministerial duties in his absence. "Minister of the Interior, Mico Stanisic." And then you see beneath the date, 21st of October, 1992.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Kovac. Mr. Kovac, during your meeting with the Chamber's Legal Officers, you indicated that you can speak to several aspects of activities of RS MUP leaders during 1992. The Chamber is interested in a very discrete issue, that of the leadership of the MUP as you may have gathered. Please bear that in mind when answering the following questions. You obviously have knowledge of far more than we intend to elicit from you today and you will have to be as brief as possible. When we need further detail, we will ask follow-up questions. And if you think there is need for further clarification, you will be provided with an opportunity to do so. Now, I want you to look at your interview of October 2003, that would be tab 1, page 28 in the English and -- well, there is again --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: -- a problem -- yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry to interrupt but the interviews of the witness are not in that binder, I'm afraid --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: The --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Because I have highlighted them --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: -- and it's in a separate binder. I'm really sorry for that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Okay. It's on the screen, Mr. Kovac, and you received a copy in B/C/S; is that right? That's your interview of October 2003. And --

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV KOVAC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: -- you refer in that interview to inappropriate staff within the RS MUP in the time Mico Stanisic was the minister. Now, my question is: Can you name a few of the individuals who you are referring to here and give me the names of the individuals with the municipalities or the areas of their responsibility.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm sorry to intervene. Even with my rudimentary B/C/S, it appears that the B/C/S page on the screen doesn't match up with the English page. Even though I see it's number -- page number 1 on the B/C/S, it appears to be referring to starting with tape 3 as opposed to the introduction.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kovac seems to -- do you know what I'm referring to, Mr. Kovac?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV KOVAC
utterances.text: No. This isn't it. I believe that there has been a mix-up. What I see now is not the first part of my interview and doesn't refer to Mr. Stanisic, but actually has to do with quite a different topic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, if I may be of assistance.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Well, yes, it is just that the pages on the monitor do not correspond and we're trying to locate the one. If this is a correct page in English that is needed, we are trying to locate it right now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: It's at line 13 of page 28 in the English and it is -- it says: "And we," so that's Mr. Kovac speaking. "We also tried to finish up what -- to finish up squaring it out or clearing out the inappropriate staff within the police stations and centres, which had begun back in times of Mico Stanisic." So ...

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, maybe it's now my turn to assist. What we now have before us in front of -- on the screen, on the right-hand side is the right page in English which Your Honour has just quoted; however, on the left side in B/C/S, this page does not correspond to what is on the right side. And now it seems that we have inversion of pages. What we have previously were both also these two pages, however, the right one was correct in B/C/S, but the English was the wrong one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kovac, can you remember telling the people that interviewed you that at the time that Mr. Stanisic was the minister of the interior there was inappropriate staff within the MUP, within the police stations and the centres?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV KOVAC
utterances.text: I really would like to see my exact words in the Serbian language, so as to avoid any ambiguity.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Okay. We'll have to put it up and find it.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think what has happened, based on what I saw, it appears on these large interviews they're often -- interpretations are done by three or four different interpreters. So if someone does tape one, someone will do tape two, et cetera. I think they've been assembled out of order because that first page seemed to be the beginning of tape 3. Perhaps if we could take a short break of ten minutes or so, with my colleagues or a language assistant in my office we might be able to more quickly find it than trying to do it ad hoc here in the courtroom. Or if you wanted to continue on to another topic and come back --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Unless Mr. Zecevic has found it?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I have found it, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I think it is page 18 in the -- it has number 18 out of 233 on it. It should be either 18 or 19 in the e-court --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Okay --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: -- in the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Can we see then or show the witness page 18. And are the lines numbered in B/C/S as well? Then, Mr. Zecevic, you could perhaps --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: It starts on page 18, line 19, and then continues on the next page.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Okay. Can you see that, Mr. Kovac?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV KOVAC
utterances.text: Yes, but we should now see whether that is what you have in mind. The question was: "What was your relationship with Mr. Rakic?" This is what I see on the screen. And then my answer follows after that question. If that's what you wanted to deal with, then we have it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: That's where I'm referring to, yes. And then at a certain moment you say in the English translation: "And we also tried to finish up what -- to finish up squaring it out or clearing out the inappropriate staff within the police station and centres which we had begun back in times of Mica Stanisic." Do you see that or do -- do we have to turn over to the next page?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV KOVAC
utterances.text: Yes, I can see it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Okay. Now, the question is: Inappropriate staff, can you be a little bit more precise? Name individuals you were referring to, individuals and eventually the municipality they were working in or the responsibilities they had?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV KOVAC
utterances.text: As far as our professional approach was concerned, the approach that we had at the time, and my interview, when I said "unfit staff" or "inappropriate" as it was translated here, I was referring to people who without the necessary ethical or professional qualities came to positions at public security stations. They were able to do so after the multi-party elections in Bosnia and Herzegovina and the then authorities, the tripartite authorities that consisted of the SDA, the SDS, and the HDZ, they at the time did not heed any professional qualities. They selected people from the ranks of the local political parties, and those were people - maybe not all of them - but certainly many of them, people that they could handle. And those were the people that they used when the war began. And these were the people at the public security stations that we inherited, as it were. People like me, who were not like them, were given the task by Mr. Stanisic to get rid of them, that is, get rid of such staff who did not act in accordance with the police codex. I initiated measures against all those who were not from the -- from the police, who didn't have the required professional or ethical mind-set.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Did you have particular people in mind when you said this or when you are explaining this now?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV KOVAC
utterances.text: Certainly, I did have some specific people in mind.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Could you tell us?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV KOVAC
utterances.text: Some of them were station chiefs. Well, talking about station chiefs, I can start from Samac, Steve. Then Bijeljina, the chief of the station there --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Samac, who are you talking about precisely, which individual?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV KOVAC
utterances.text: I'm talking about - what was his name? - Steve or Stevan Todorovic, he's the one I'm talking about. And then the public security station of Prijedor, I think the one who was there was Simo Drljaca.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Okay. You mentioned --

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV KOVAC
utterances.text: I think that at Pale itself - although I didn't mention that - there were also dismissals. That was at the time when I came there. There were a number of public security stations such as Zvornik, I can't remember the name of the man there, but there were a number of stations where people had to be replaced. And all those who didn't really have control of the police in their stations but tolerated or were in practice replaced by para-police units there. We also wanted to replace --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kovac, you mentioned Bijeljina. Any individual in particular there?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV KOVAC
utterances.text: Unfortunately there was some people who had come from Sarajevo, such as Dragan Andan. There were also local staff there, the local police station commander who was not capable of coping with -- but I can't remember his name now. The first centre chief there, he was also a local at the time, but I can't recall his name at the moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: And --

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV KOVAC
utterances.text: Anyway, I'm talking about --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: And for Pale, you have a name for Pale?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV KOVAC
utterances.text: I know that we spoke about that. I don't know whether Stanisic had already replaced him. That was the MUP headquarters there. I believe that in order to honour the legality of work that the public security station chief had to be replaced, but not because of war crimes or anything like that but in order to make sure that the station functioned properly. I don't remember when exactly it happened, but there were also activities for the purpose of replacing the station chief at Pale and in other stations too. There was a process, in the framework of which where I'm sure we replaced at least 50 of the per cent of the staff or at least we had rotated them, because there is this procedure of rotating staff from one function or position to another.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: The names you mention are all people from police stations. Any people from CSBs? Any people in particular from CSBs?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV KOVAC
utterances.text: Certainly. Yes, certainly from CSBs. I mentioned the Bijeljina centre. I can't remember the name of the man, but there were acting officers. I don't know whether there was Dragan Andan, but the situation in Bijeljina was unclear. The same applies to Banja Luka, the Banja Luka CSB where there was Stojan Zupljanin, and I had this opinion of him too because my assessment was that he was unable to control the situation and cope with the chiefs of public security stations in Krajina. And there was also the need for more integration between the centres and the stations. The process had already been well under way and I believe that it also concerned the centre chief in Sarajevo. A centre in Zvornik was being established, there was reorganisation, so that there was this broad process, the purpose of which was to set up the full jurisdiction of the Ministry of the Interior and make sure the proper functioning of the ministry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for the Judge, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: I'm sorry. Mr. Kovac, the people who in your view or in the minister's view were not only incompetent but were also misbehaving, how did -- well, let me, first of all, ask you when did you learn about the activities of these people?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV KOVAC
utterances.text: I would like to correct you. There was not only the category of unfit people. There was also the category of those who were unable to cope and have the centres, public security centres, under their control, who didn't have the power. In the ministry especially at times of war you cannot --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kovac, I'm -- I do make that distinction, but I wanted to focus now on those who were not only incompetent and could not control their organisation, but I want to focus on the ones who misbehaved and who were -- towards whom you were taking action because of that. So my question is for those people, how -- when did you learn about their misbehaviour?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV KOVAC
utterances.text: I couldn't pin-point a date. It was a process. When I was appointed to my position, Stanisic stated the reasons to me. He knew my profile as a police officer. He knew that right before the war I was a chairman of the disciplinary board for the Sarajevo region, and he made it clear to me that he wanted me to set up a CSB in Bijeljina and that we monitored the legality of work through the administrations and check all staff - what they did and how they went about it - and replace some staff by more competent people so that the ministry could carry out its tasks at those difficult times when there was intense combat in that civil war, when all the values of the previous states and societies had been destroyed and law and order had to be established, and that was up to us. That's why we needed strong people and strong institutions. And from that aspect and from that level that we assessed the -- whether somebody was fit or unfit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kovac, what I want to make clear here about when you learned about this, in your answer you say this was in the process when I was the assistant minister, so not before that period that you learned about this; right?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV KOVAC
utterances.text: Before that I was at Ilidza where there was intensive combat activity, and I didn't have specific information about events elsewhere. When Stanisic --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: That's a clear answer. My follow-up question is then so now we're talking again about the time you were in the position of assistant minister. How did you learn about these activities of the -- or this misbehaviour? What was the reporting chain, I suppose, that went up the reporting chain and then -- and reach you in your capacity as assistant minister; is that right? So what was the reporting chain?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV KOVAC
utterances.text: What I found out officially about the problems that I faced in the ministry, I found out at the collegium of the Ministry of the Interior in Trebinje, I believe it was held in August. That is when the centre chiefs and their deputies outlined the situation and the problems in the territory of the then-Republika Srpska as well as within the ministry itself. When I moved on, or rather, when I went to Bijeljina at the same time I set up a group of co-workers, inspectors, who were the embryo of the institution of public security. And we launched the process of reporting to the organisational unit of the ministry in Bijeljina. We received information about whether or not public security stations worked in accordance with the law, both from the inspectors and from the public security or security services centres.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kovac, can you please look at tab number 6, which is P160, at page 7, please. And my question is: Is this the kind of meeting where you and the minister would be briefed at?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, probably yes, although I haven't had the opportunity to deal with this. I don't remember this specific document, but this is a way of reporting -- actually, these are more analyses and presentation of the directions of activity. This is not the kind of document where daily reporting or reporting about daily activities was made. Could we -- could I see it until the end?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: You're completely right, Mr. Kovac. It's -- the document is called "Brief analysis of the work to date and basic guide-lines for the future work of the MUP." It's a summary from the meeting of the MUP senior officials of the 11 of July, 1992. Now, could you please look at page 8 and then 14 of that document. There is reference -- reference is made there to crimes being committed by men in uniforms, and both Mr. Zupljanin at page 8 and Mr. Stanisic at page 14 say that the courts are not properly functioning. Was this a concern throughout 1992?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV KOVAC
utterances.text: Certainly. This was a great problem, but we continued our activities. As far as all such events are concerned, we already had an analysis in Bijeljina. I don't think I was present at this meeting, though, because I don't remember it. Probably I couldn't attend. But I know that we, or rather, that I sent a document to the president of the republic and the cabinet about this very topic so that some things that have to do with the functioning of the courts be dealt with.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: We'll come to that, Mr. Kovac. Just to be complete and for the record, the document and the meeting you were referring to before we got into this one is in your binder at tab 22 and it is Exhibit Number P163. Can we pull that up. And then, Mr. Kovac, could you confirm that that's the document and the meeting you were referring to before we got to this one?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV KOVAC
utterances.text: Yes, this is a document from the meeting in Trebinje, and I officially started attending executive meetings as of that date because before I wasn't in attendance.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Now then, when you came into the top MUP administration, what did you find was the policy of the -- or the attitude towards individuals such as those we are now talking about and who were unfit for their task and, more specifically, who were misbehaving? What was the policy or the attitude within the MUP towards those people?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV KOVAC
utterances.text: Well, starting from this senior officials' meeting in Trebinje, I clearly remember that all the participants were aware that the process was already launched in order to eradicate all the flaws within the MUP as well as in other institutions and the society in general Republika Srpska. Therefore, my feeling was that I already became part of that process. And the second part of my involvement was my suggestion to Mr. Stanisic to tackle the matter of decision-makers because the existing personnel were unable to do that, that we needed a more efficient and more decisive people from the level of the ministry all the way down to police stations. So there was no doubt as to what to do with these people. The only problematic thing was whether there was a will or whether there was enough strength to deal and to bring into light all the personnel problems and to resolve all the personnel issues which required some radical moves on the part of the police in order to make it fully operational in the area of public law and order, the protection of property, the protection of other ethnicities, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, before the break we can perhaps deal with one other document issue. One of the first things you did when you took up your position in August 1992 was to make a recommendation directly to the president and prime minister with -- on how to deal with prisoners. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV KOVAC
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct, but I only signed it. This recommendation was actually put together by the ministry, so I didn't have any significant contribution in it. It was just the outcome of an analysis.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Let's perhaps look at a document, please. It's P192 and it's tab 7 in your binder, Mr. Kovac. Is that the letter we're talking about?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV KOVAC
utterances.text: Yes, that's the letter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Okay. How would you describe your relationship with Mico Stanisic in 1992?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV KOVAC
utterances.text: Well, we had a decent relationship in the course of 1992, which was reflected in his providing support to me with regard to all the activities that we became involved as the public security service in order to redress all these problems. He never made any obstacles. He let us go all through to the end. Unfortunately, we didn't have enough strength and also he didn't have enough political strength to see this through.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kovac, in your October 2003 interview you said about your relationship with Mico Stanisic, if I'm not mistaken, that you were always - you and him - you were always on good terms. You confirm that? We're talking about your relationship in 1992. Is that correct, you were on good terms, is that --

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV KOVAC
utterances.text: Well, given that we are different personalities, I wouldn't say that we were on exactly good terms. We were professionally on good terms, so in -- during his second term of office there appeared some disagreements, but before that we saw eye to eye in the professional sense when it became -- when it came to how the service should be run. And I can say that in that I had his full support.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Now, my follow-up question on your, let's say, good professional relationship with Mr. Stanisic is: Why did you send the letter we still have on the screen, I think, directly to the president and the prime minister instead of addressing it to Mr. Stanisic, who was your hierarchical superior, he was your boss?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV KOVAC
utterances.text: Well, first of all, there was no need for me to communicate with Stanisic in this manner because we managed to agree on many things. As far as this letter is concerned, I saw it as a reflection of the tasks that we had in Trebinje and as a reflection of the entire set of activities that needed to be carried out. So the motive for sending this letter was not to circumvent Stanisic - it wasn't possible after all - but I was convinced that what we were doing and the letter that I sent is the outcome of our overall activities. In the ministry, Stanisic set up things in such a manner that quite a lot of tasks he delegated and allowed me to do on his behalf. So by sending this letter - and we never had any dispute over it - was the -- not so the product of my conviction as to what I should do or shouldn't do, but rather, it had to do with the circumstances that were in place at the time and the place where Stanisic was. Therefore, the content of this letter and the proposals that were made at the senior executive staff meeting in Trebinje contain no differences. My sole wish was to do things as quickly as possible, and this is in line with Mr. Trbojevic, the vice prime minister, and I was often in communication with him. There was a need to introduce speedy measures, and this is the purpose of this letter. So the time was like this and I was such a person who thought that one should act rapidly and speedily and that certain measures needed to be done immediately. After all, the government adopted this into its document and introduced certain measures. So nothing was done by bypassing anyone --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Okay. We'll have to discuss a little bit more this document, but perhaps we should do that after the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: We resume in 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Okay. This is supposed to work now and it does, obviously. Mr. Kovac, before the break you seemed to indicate that this document, that you signed it but it was not really your initiative, your decision. It was something the administration prepared for you. Was that what you're saying? Because it seems a little bit -- I don't read that in your interviews. You seem to say in your interviews that it's something you thought would be a good idea and that you did take the decision and present it as a good solution. Can you clarify on that?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV KOVAC
utterances.text: I think there's a slight misunderstanding. What I meant to say was that the final version of this information is the product of the activities of the entire ministry. It was me, indeed, who established this in this form and sent this letter as it is to the government and the Presidency. In other words, I stand by it 100 per cent. But this is not a simple letter. This is analysis of all our activities and our intentions --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Okay. I just wanted to clarify this little point, but you did it perfectly. Now, could you please explain what you meant when you recommended that the status of members of other ethnicities be legally altered in accordance with international conventions. What did you have in mind exactly?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV KOVAC
utterances.text: Look, I think that this question that you asked me and the proposals that we made are actually a key element and a key moment in this civil war. And if you allow me to clarify, I would like just to be given a little bit more time on this specific issue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV KOVAC
utterances.text: The essence of this - and I'm going to input my professional knowledge into this - the essence of the behaviour of people in a civil war where you have a mixture of civilians of various ethnicities and in addition to that you have armed people fighting each other, and in Bosnia-Herzegovina there was not a third power, a central government, a central army that would separate or reconcile the warring parties. So each and every ethnic group - and I'm talking now about the Serbian side - had to establish or reinstate the values that had been lost. We had to establish an army and we had to reintroduce a set of values that have to be respected by warring parties. And I think these were the most difficult tasks, that is, to reinforce our institutions and our decisions and the awareness that among the warring parties in a civil war there was enough strength to distinguish between the civilians, the people who didn't have any uniforms, and of course also to distinguish a third group, which is criminals who were committing criminal offences. In a civil war, everybody thinks that it is only the opposing side who committed all the crimes and that it attacked the civilians. And I think that this is a phenomenon that is present in every civil war. I believe that these were exactly the stages in a war that required our efforts to strengthen the Ministry of the Interior, the judiciary, and all other institutions in order for them to be able to wrestle with this problem. So as a result of these negative processes and these awful things that were happening in Bosnia when you had a mixed population, ethnically mixed populations, where you had people armed among different ethnic communities, the issue of the laws that govern the relation and the treatment of prisoners of war and the criminal offenders, et cetera, is something that is extremely difficult. And I think it was nearly impossible to resolve that and eventually this necessitated the creation of this Tribunal, among other things. So this realisation contributed to us trying to go a step forward and to try to solve these problems. As you can see, this document is officially registered and it is officially being sent to both the government and all other relevant representatives. So if you look at this document and look at its purpose, by making it official it means that at those times we had lengthy discussions about what was to be done, but that was done outside the institutions. In this instance, the MUP as an institution is sending an official document to the president of the republic and the prime minister. And of course, in this document we had to highlight exactly everything that was happening. In my subsequent talks with Mr. Trbojevic, the vice-president of the republic, the government acted quickly and adopted a series of very specific measures aimed at eradicating these behaviours and to ensure that the institutions, such as judiciary, correctional and prisoner facilities and other institutions, have a clear vision as to how they should act in accordance with these three guide-lines. After analysing what needs to be done, I concluded that we need to construe the basic provisions contained in the law with regard to categorisation of people into the category who cannot be responsible for being member of a certain ethnic group. Then you have prisoners of war, and everybody knows how they should be treated; and a third category of those who may have committed criminal offences.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: So --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: Could the witness for the benefit of the interpreters and the court reporter kindly be asked to speak more slowly. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kovac, the interpreters ask whether you could speak slower so that they can -- they have the better possibility of making correct translations. Now -- so I take it from your answer that what you are doing here is you try to work something out for people detained that were not combatants and that did not commit any crimes, who were detained because they committed any crimes. And your solution was to categorise them as refugees; is that right? Is that a fair summary?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV KOVAC
utterances.text: Well, our proposal was that they be afforded the status of civilians. Now, depending on whether they remained in their homes and their native places, those were civilian populations. However, if they were moved as a result of war operations and found themselves elsewhere, they should definitely be given the status either of displaced persons or refugees, depending on how they were treated and perceived. So this was the option given to free people who should be taken care of by the Red Cross and not government organs. But at any rate, they shouldn't be treated in such a manner as to restrict their freedom of movement and to judge them as possible perpetrators of crimes. So that was the main direction that we took. Now, as to the actual organisation and the accommodation and other facilities, it was decided on the spot. So as for the civilians, there are two subgroups: Those who remained home in their houses and residential places and those who moved elsewhere. So this is something that came out through our co-operation with international organisations, humanitarian organisations; and in view of that, we made such a proposal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Just one small clarification. When you say -- when you made a difference between depending on whether they remained in their homes and their native places and you qualified them as civilian population; however, you said if they were moved as a result of war operations and found themselves elsewhere - and that's the second category - if they were moved as a result of war operations and found themselves elsewhere, that's a description of people being -- of the people being detained. We are talking about detained people; right?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV KOVAC
utterances.text: No, no, no. It is precisely why we provided this information that the people who left the area can in no way be treated as detainees. They can only be treated as civilians and that the Red Cross should become involved and provide them support in terms of accommodation and other forms of assistance, food, et cetera. And then, depending on what their future decisions would be, they would remain in the area where they came or they would move to third countries. So the civilian population was treated in such a way that it should be exclusively in the care of the government and authorities and humanitarian organisations.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kovac, that is the goal you had, the purpose for which you wrote this letter and made this suggestion. But it is -- I understand it is about people who, before you made this suggestion, are not in their homes anymore but are detained in camps; right? And you tried to - that's what you say and what you explain about this letter - you tried to give a solution to that problem. Is that correctly understood?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV KOVAC
utterances.text: In this letter we requested the government authorities to take a clear position regarding the categorisation of individuals, and then if we saw on the ground that there were categories that did not comply with international conventions, this proposal and the request by the government to undertake urgent measures and to apply a proper legal treatment of these people, so if they were put in certain correctional penal facilities, that should have been taken care of. We received information that there were instances in which civilians were not treated in an appropriate manner. And as the MUP, who is the first port of call when we receive this kind of information, we thought it necessary to inform the president and the prime minister immediately and that measures should be taken at once. I think that this was one of the crucial institutional moves that would put a stop to all these negative aspects and misconduct, which undoubtedly did happen, but depending on how powerful an individual or an institution was, we did our best to eliminate all these negative aspects which were definitely an outcome of civil war and conduct of individuals. Whether that can be attributed to their ignorance or whether you can attribute it to their mental constitution, that's a different matter. I remember that after the government took its decision for certain correctional and penal facilities --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: I'll come to that, Mr. Kovac. I was just trying to figure out whether we now agree or not on my question, and my question pertained to not what your request was to the government, what your proposed solution was, but what the problem was you tried to tackle. And the problem was, as you've said, that people from the civilian population were not treated correctly and that that should stop. And in clear, being not treated correctly meant being detained although civilians with no combatant status and no crimes committed. That's a summary of the reason why you requested this to the government. Do we agree on that? That's the problem you tried to solve.

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV KOVAC
utterances.text: Yes, partly. The basic problem was during all those operations that were going on, there was no fast and adequate separation between the civilian population and the members of fighting units or prisoners of war who had committed crimes. There was no efficient and adequate approach to that, and I explained to you how those processes went. Due to that inadequate separation, there was also inadequate treatment sometimes of those persons. If we hadn't -- or, rather, the fact that we didn't notice the problem back then was the reason for the proposal made to the state structures in order to bring about treatment that was in accordance with the law and the circumstances of civil war. But there were not enough trained people in the state bodies, or especially in the political structures, trained for acting in civil war. I don't mean combat now, but I mean -- I'm referring to internal structures under specific circumstances where ethnicities are in conflict although they live maybe in the same village.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Kovac, now I would like to take the next step and ask you what was done precisely to implement your suggestion, if it was implemented? What was the follow-up on it? What measures were taken?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV KOVAC
utterances.text: I think that the most important measure that was taken was the following. The deputy prime minister for the interior whose remit included the MUP and the judiciary - and I'm talking about Mr. Trbojevic - he called a cabinet session. I don't want to go into the way the government functioned, but I know that he called that session. And there was an item on the agenda about this very report of the MUP, including proposed measures. That's -- that was the follow-up. I noticed that you have these decisions at your disposal. It followed very soon. I don't think it took more than ten days when this item was dealt with by the government, namely, the report of the MUP.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Okay. Can we please look at P193, which is tab 8 in your binder. It's an order issued by Trbojevic on behalf of Prime Minister Djeric. Is that the follow-up you're talking about or part of the follow-up you're talking about? Is that the response to your letter?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV KOVAC
utterances.text: I cannot state with certainty that this was part of the response to my letter, but I know that this was part of the activities that we carried out. I know that there was this cabinet session. This is about part of the activities we were engaged in, but I cannot be specific as to your question. Maybe this followed the letter or preceded it or went parallel to it. I know that this inspector carried out audits. I know of these activities, but I cannot be specific as to the chronology.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Okay. Can we then look at tab 8A, which is Exhibit Number P601. Was this the commission that we saw in the decision, the decision tab 8, was this commission effectively formed? Was it established?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV KOVAC
utterances.text: This is a commission of the security centre. I think that the government commission had a different composition. I believe that it was set up later, the government commission. I see that this is a commission of the security services centre and it consists of inspectors from that centre, and they were touring the stations.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Okay --

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV KOVAC
utterances.text: This is the process of establishing the situation on the ground. They went there and informed us what --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Can we --

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV KOVAC
utterances.text: The government issued a special decision about the setting up of their commission --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Can we now --

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV KOVAC
utterances.text: This is a decision of the security services centre --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kovac, can we turn to tab 9, the next tab, Exhibit Number 2D90, and can I ask you: Have you seen this before?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I cannot read the document well --

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, if I may be of some assistance. I mean, I have just noticed that Mr. Kovac is looking at the screen right in front of him and I believe it would be much easier for him to have a hard copy. He does have it, this binder. So maybe if he can turn to what Your Honour just said, the document which is under number 9 in his tab.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Just one moment, Mr. Kovac. We might have a problem with the numbers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Okay. Could we try to turn to page 26 of this document, 2D90.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for the Judge, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: I'm sorry. So we turn to page 26 of 2D90, and it states that the Prijedor SJB provides to the commission the information it requires for its investigation and it is signed by Simo Drljaca. We don't see that here but we can show that at the end of the document, the last page.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: There it is with Simo Drljaca's handwritten signature. So my question would be, if you know: Was Mr. Drljaca assisting that commission? Was he assisting with the commission's work at -- in Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV KOVAC
utterances.text: Well, you see, I cannot comment on that, but since I have this hard copy before me from my first report all the way to the government decision - and it's in neat chronological order - and therefore it can clearly be seen how the process went through these commissions and all. So we launched a process which was clearly painful and we pointed out everything that was bad, all the shortcomings in the work. And it can clearly be seen how much they deviated from the attitude of the ministry with regard to the treatment of civilians and prisoners and so on. It is clear from all these reports what the situation was on the ground and the chronology is clear. From the 8th of August, the proposal of the MUP to the government, after which there was the decision, the government decision. After that, there was the decision of the centre chiefs about the setting up of the commissions, and the commission reports. It is clear that we launched a process and it is clear that not everything was impeccable. We are not shying away from that fact. But still, we did something to rectify all that wasn't all right. There were professionals involved, inspectors - after the war they became inspectors and before the war they must also have been in positions, whether you worked responsibly. It is clear that they mustered all their strength to come up with reports pin-pointing everything that was bad and showing that there were many shortcomings in the work. There was -- there were the Crisis Staffs, there was the conduct of some people, and everything else. As for Simo Drljaca, I didn't receive any information about his relations with the commission. If I never got reports about him, then I couldn't know how he acted in any given situation. I don't know whether he obstructed or not. But irrespective of that, the commissions did their work, which is clear from the report.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Can we have page 25, please, where it says that the -- the commission's report is based on the reports received from the SJB of Bosanski Novi as well. So that seems to be part of the process; right?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV KOVAC
utterances.text: Certainly, it's part of the process.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: So this was how the commission obtained its information and conducted its investigation. What comes in mind, isn't that not the report then written by the people who were supposed to be investigated upon?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV KOVAC
utterances.text: Yes. Well, you see, let me explain. With regard to many territories of the RS, we had no influence over them, either physical or through government structures. If we take the Krajina, if you look at a number of these documents, then you will see a government decision, then a decision of the centre chief, then -- and there's little mention of the Ministry of the Interior. So much lay with the security services centre, and the units on the ground were so independent that rarely did anybody dare to go there and conduct an audit, let alone deal with these matters which were the most sensitive and which could incriminate the people in those stations. We did launch this process, though, and the most important thing regarding this is that after that process this sort of conduct was eliminated. And we certainly identified through this process what had happened and what the attitude of some individuals toward these matters was. And I'm now referring to the most serious problem in this territory during that civil war. I mean it can clearly be seen that since launching the process or by launching the process we forced the station chiefs to co-operate and give information about the events in their territory. And in their reports, they drew a picture of themselves. They do their own profile and showed their attitude toward the ministry and everything else. There's not much to add to these reports. I really don't have anything to add to them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: One clarification question. This commission, was it only appointed for the area under CSB Banja Luka or in other municipalities as well?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV KOVAC
utterances.text: I think that this commission covered the territory of the Banja Luka CSB, as far as I can tell from this. It was set up for that CSB. And objectively speaking, at that time the most problems with treatment of civilian population were to be found there, because that's where most people who are of other ethnicities lived, in the area around Banja Luka and all the way to Doboj, and that was the greatest portion, almost 80 per cent of the territory.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Okay, then. Are you aware of what precise action was taken following the submission of the report of -- the report of this commission?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV KOVAC
utterances.text: Well, first of all, the Ministry of the Interior and the public security stations distanced themselves very soon from such an unnecessary treatment of the population. They distanced themselves from all sorts of centres and correctional facilities and the like. Wherever we went -- and the process was basically finished at the time. Anyway, at that point in time, we had no more information that such activity was no longer possible there and those centres were disappearing. Pursuant to some measures taken by the government these centres were being closed. They were no longer there as institutions or para-institutions. This process involved a number of activities and the commissions themselves acted in a preventive manner. The police officers came to their senses and it was no longer possible to induct the professional police into -- or maybe in exceptional cases where we -- about which we didn't know anything. So it was no longer possible for them to be involved in such activities.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kovac, apart from all that, was there any specific action taken against people who were responsible for the conditions in these circumstances, in these detention camps and centres? Was there any action taken against responsible people?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV KOVAC
utterances.text: All centre chiefs were given the task, because it comes under the remit of the first-instance body, to take measures, disciplinary measures, that is, and possibly also launch criminal proceedings. That was the duty of every centre chief, and they were able to take a stance or -- by their activities and by possibly filing criminal complaints. They had the documents at their disposal about all these persons. I cannot now go into specific cases. We sometimes directly intervened and arrested individuals - we from the ministry headquarters I mean - when there was some illegal activities. So we did some things directly. Where an assessment already existed and when there was a situation that could no longer be tolerated, then we took immediate action. I'm referring to the specific case of Todorovic in Bijeljina. We were directly involved in that during that initial period. Although, when we set up the administrations, we got more involved in audits of the centres and personnel-related processes were underway there, people were being replaced. I believe that this was stopped in 1993, unfortunately, when Ratko Adzic became minister --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kovac, please don't wander off too far. You said that the chiefs -- the centre chiefs were given the task to take disciplinary measures and so on, launch criminal proceedings. Did you on the level of the ministry do any follow-up on whether the centre chiefs executed these tasks? Do you know of disciplinary measures taken by the centre chiefs or criminal proceedings launched?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV KOVAC
utterances.text: I can say that as the process established in the administrations progressed, we monitored them more and more. However, at the very CSBs there wasn't enough power or strength to carry the burden of these problems and to solve them finally - due to the war or maybe to some other circumstances - but nevertheless, they were unable to carry out the process through. That is to say, to hold people accountable, to institute criminal proceedings, et cetera. This is my personal view, that they were not strong enough and they didn't have acumen enough to do that. In January 1993 this process lost its edge and it was eventually stopped. At the time I was a pro forma assistant minister, and for the following nine months, we faced a total blockade of the operation of the Ministry of the Interior while Mr. Adzic, the -- Mr. Stanisic's successor was in his office. I don't know if you understood my answer. So in August and September we launched a series of activities, but only a few months later - that is to say, on the 1st of January - a political decision was made to install a new minister who didn't have professional credibility to do the job or any other mental capabilities to do that as far as my department is concerned; and as a result, he put all the activities to a halt and he put the ministry in such a difficult position that there was confrontation between administrations on the one hand and the CSBs on the other hand. And it reached its peak at one of the meetings of the executive staff and the ministry almost totally disintegrated during his term of office. So that was the reason why we were forced to stop all these activities.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Okay. I would like to go back a little bit. If you would like to, please, look at tape -- at tab 9A, which is P679.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Have you seen this document before?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV KOVAC
utterances.text: I cannot remember seeing it. I see that this document was drafted on behalf of Simo Drljaca, but I can't remember exactly whether I have seen this document or not. And I don't see any link or any communication here with the MUP. This is a letter coming from the public security station of Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Can you tell us whether this was something that resulted from the report of that commission? And I'm referring to --

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV KOVAC
utterances.text: Yes, I think that it did result. Yes, of course, this is a result and it depicts certain activities as ordered by the minister of the interior.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. Now, at pages 151 and 201 of your October 2003 interview, you said that Simo Drljaca was beyond the control of the MUP in 1992. What did you mean by saying he ran Prijedor on his own and that you had to breakthrough the CSB Banja Luka --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If we can go back to the previous document to look at the signature, you can see that it wasn't signed by Simo Drljaca but somebody did that instead of him. This demonstrates his overall attitude towards all these activities. Maybe the CSB of Banja Luka should be asked as a whole to tell whether he was capable of carrying out their duties. On the other hand, we were completely physically separated from the Banja Luka centre until the corridor was open. So, in fact, we did not have any physical access to the Banja Luka centre and Prijedor in particular. For that reason, it was impossible to impose the jurisdiction of the MUP over them, let alone engage some more repressive forces such as special units that we had already been using in eastern part of Republika Srpska in order to control the conduct of para groups and individuals out of control. So this is my interpretation why it was impossible for us to reach the public security station of Prijedor. There was a physical barrier; but on the other hand, we also had a barrier which was erected in general with regard to the jurisdiction of the MUP. I thought it to be, at least at the beginning, of more declaratory than factual nature. Having in view the previous system and regime, I perceived this subordination to be more solid and something that demanded the undertaking of much faster measures. Now we had quite a lot of correspondence going to and fro between the chiefs because they had some -- probably some hunch that they were each and every one of them a government per se. And our intention and our efforts were to place the whole area under our jurisdiction. I also think that the Banja Luka centre either did not have a proper position. Maybe they'd not share my opinion, but it's up to them to prove that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Let's try to get a little bit more precise about this, Mr. Kovac. Can we have 151 in the English version and 173 in the B/C/S version on the screen, the October 2003 interview. Because my question was two-fold, Mr. Kovac. It was: What did you mean by saying Simo Drljaca ran Prijedor on his own? And on the other hand, what did you mean by saying that you had to breakthrough the CSB Banja Luka? And if I remember correctly - let me just have a look --

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV KOVAC
utterances.text: As --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Just one moment, please.

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV KOVAC
utterances.text: May I?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: No, not yet. Here it is. I'm having in mind -- you said on page 2 -- on page 150: "I'm having in mind Banja Luka and Prijedor, until we literally got into the Banja Luka centre or actually breakthrough the Banja Luka centre and until we had Stojan Zupljanin and his associates dismissed as the MUP centre. We had no jurisdiction over there." So my question is: What did you mean by that in relation to Simo Drljaca and in relation to Stojan Zupljanin?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV KOVAC
utterances.text: Well, when I said that we virtually broke into it refers to September 1993. As you know, in September 1993 there was a rebellion among the army in Banja Luka. And one of the offences that they committed was that these military units took complete hold of the CSB Banja Luka in a manner that they entered all the premises of both the state and public security services. They misappropriated all the equipment and all the assets that were there on the premises. So what we had there was a total militarisation and the total deprivation of the MUP to carry out these duties. Any official of the MUP was not allowed to even approach close to that centre. Now, in order to quell this rebellion and this uprising against the state with some ten people from the state security and some 30 special forces from the centre of MUP, we managed to arrest the ring-leaders of the rebellion and that is when we physically entered --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kovac, excuse me, excuse me, but unless I'm very wrong, this would not be the reason or this would not justify your opinion that you had to dismiss Stojan Zupljanin and his associates. Isn't that right? That has nothing to do with a military rebellion. So my question was about this opinion of yours, that before you could do something you had to dismiss Stojan Zupljanin and his associates.

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV KOVAC
utterances.text: Maybe I was giving you a much too lengthy answer. At the time when the CSB Banja Luka was completely thrown out of the system as a result of the rebellion, we physically entered the centre. And since the centre had no function at all and there were no executives there, we left it all to the commissions. At the time, Stojan Zupljanin was unable to run the centre, so that was the sequence of events. A few months later his dismissal was only confirmed and we restored the functioning of the centre by employing such personnel that would establish good links between the MUP and the CSB, because I always believed that to be the best option and it proved to be correct before and after. Because without proper connections with the MUP, no CSB can be sustainable and cannot operate under the law. So at the time, Stojan Zupljanin lost his position at the time and he eventually had to be removed. This was later confirmed by Stanisic and Rakic and they said that Zupljanin could not have stayed in position because of the issue of jurisdiction vis-a-vis the MUP, and because I personally believe him unable to govern such a big and complex area covered by the CSB Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you. I think this is a convenient point, yes, indeed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: So we take our second break to resume in 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Okay, Mr. Kovac, we -- I think you did a very good job in the beginning of your testimony by giving short answers, but probably due to the fact that this is a tiring exercise you lost a little bit of focus. I'm afraid we are having a little bit of a time problem. So if I could ask you to focus again on the precise questions and, as far as possible, give short answers. I want to go back for a minute to Simo Drljaca of whom you said that in 1992 he was beyond the control of the MUP. My question is: According to you, who had the authority to discipline him? In 1992, I mean.

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV KOVAC
utterances.text: The authority to discipline him according to the Law on the Interior, it was the chief of the Banja Luka CSB because he belonged to that centre.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Okay. And have you any explanation as to why that did not happen, why he was not disciplined, while obviously -- yeah, go ahead.

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV KOVAC
utterances.text: I think that the then chief of the centre didn't have either personal or political power to settle the scores with Simo Drljaca and everybody else because that would imply having political power and the power to deal with the entire Crisis Staff. And in my view, the chief of the centre didn't have such capacity, either in political terms or otherwise, and I also have doubts about how courageous he was to become involved in such a conflict. As I said, that was what was required in order to deal with him and the entire Crisis Staff. One had to really have proper political power and all other capacities required.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you. In your interview of October 2003, page 28 - and I'm looking for the B/C/S page number, I don't seem to have it on the my list -- no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: It's page 18 in the B/C/S version. Thank you. You said that you, along with others, dismissed those responsible for crimes in 1992, including Simo Drljaca. Can you please clarify when you took this action?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV KOVAC
utterances.text: I can't understand which part of my interview are you referring to or are you just asking me a question that stems from my interview?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: It stems from your interview. You said in your interview that you dismissed those responsible for crimes in 1992 and that was including Simo Drljaca. And the rather simple question is, if you remember, is a question to clarify when you dismissed the people responsible for crimes in 1992.

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV KOVAC
utterances.text: As I already said, this happened both in the latter part of 1992 and then in the first half of 1993 and then again in 1994 when Stanisic and Rakic as his deputy came. Now speaking about Simo Drljaca specifically, we managed to neutralise his powers and influence in the area; however, under enormous political pressure he managed again to resurrect. I don't know exactly when. So we had this wrangling with Drljaca the whole time, but he was politically much too strong to be completely eliminated politically. Concerning Todorovic of Samac, I know that we arrested him I think in 1993, yes, he was arrested in 1993, and we removed him. There were other chiefs as well. In 1992 I think that we removed Dragan Andan, the chief from Visegrad, and quite a few others. So this is as specific as I can be by giving you these names.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you. In -- you say "we." You also say "we" in the interview. The first question is: In what capacity did you take this action, and who are you referring to when you say "we"?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV KOVAC
utterances.text: All the steps that I took I firmly stand behind that and I would always tell you that it was me personally who did this. However, I always have the need to mention the institution because our intention and the intention of MUP was always to have a proper institution. But as I said, I stand by each and every action that I myself did, especially when I took the decision or signed the decision because the responsibility lies with the decision-maker under the law. I didn't want to emphasise "I." That's why I used the pronoun "we" because I preferred to speak on the behalf of the institution, but I would like to underline that the decisions I took were mine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Okay. Then my question is: In what capacity did you take this decision, as assistant minister? As acting minister? Is there a difference to be made?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV KOVAC
utterances.text: Only in two capacities, when I was assistant minister in 1992 and I had the authorisation by Minister Stanisic; and in the other capacity when I was acting minister from September 1993 till January 1994. Of course also at the time when I was the minister in 1995, that was in the latter half of 1995.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Let's take the very precise example of Simo Drljaca. The formal authority to discipline him, who would that be?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV KOVAC
utterances.text: Under the -- or given the organisation that existed then, it would have been the chief of the Banja Luka centre. That was in place until 1994.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: And the formal authority --

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV KOVAC
utterances.text: Let me explain. The proposal to launch disciplinary proceedings under the laws and regulations that existed then - and I was chairman of the disciplinary board before the war - could come from any staff member of the administration that controlled the work of the Prijedor CSB. So the initiative didn't have to come from the centre chief. It could also come from others, inspectors and so on. And the centre chief was duty-bound to implement the first-instance disciplinary proceedings.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Okay. The formal authority to dismiss Simo Drljaca, who would that be? Or -- no, let me just stay there for the moment. Who was the formal authority who could dismiss Drljaca, as happened?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV KOVAC
utterances.text: Drljaca could be dismissed by the minister of the interior as the result of second-instance proceedings. If such proceedings were implemented and the decision confirmed, that had to come from the minister himself. If that went through disciplinary proceedings. If some other proceedings were in place or consensual termination, for example. But then again it was -- it came under the remit of the minister of the interior according to the then law. The minister who was the head of a state body - in this case the minister of the interior - was the one person who had to make the decisions on both accepting people into service and dismissing them from service. That was prescribed by the Law on Internal Affairs.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: So then your decision to dismiss Simo Drljaca was taken either acting as a minister or minister as such, not as an assistant minister. You couldn't do that as an assistant minister. You could do that as an assistant minister acting on behalf of the minister; right?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV KOVAC
utterances.text: That is right, but I think I could elaborate only based on a specific document. Certainly the transfer of authority was sufficient - I mean the authority of the minister of the interior - was sufficient to dismiss somebody from the service formally speaking, if that's what you mean.
